scenes.tts: The vagus looks like one grey cable, running from the body up to the brainstem. Does it carry one message, or many?
scenes.visual: Title card: Three Questions, Not One. A single grey cable runs from a mouse body outline up to a brainstem. Question on screen: one message, or many?
scenes.narration: The vagus looks like one grey cable, running from the body up to the brainstem. Does it carry one message, or many?

scenes.tts: A sensory fibre that carries signals from the body toward the brain is called an afferent.
scenes.visual: The cable resolves into separate fibres, each with an arrow pointing upward, toward the brainstem. Label: afferent, body to brain.
scenes.narration: A sensory fibre that carries signals from the body toward the brain is called an afferent.

scenes.tts: The sense of the body's own internal state is interoception. Lung volume, blood pressure, how full the gut is.
scenes.visual: Three small organ icons beside the fibres: a lung, an artery, a stomach. Label: interoception, the body's internal state.
scenes.narration: The sense of the body's own internal state is interoception. Lung volume, blood pressure, how full the gut is.

scenes.tts: Here is the result that starts the lesson. Light on one set of vagal afferents stops an anaesthetized mouse breathing.
scenes.visual: A thin light fibre over an exposed nerve. One subset of axons glows gold. A breathing trace below is suppressed.
scenes.narration: Here is the result that starts the lesson. Light on one set of vagal afferents stops an anaesthetized mouse breathing.

scenes.tts: Light on another set, in the same nerve, makes it breathe fast and shallow.
scenes.visual: Matched second panel. A different subset glows gold; the breathing trace becomes rapid and small.
scenes.narration: Light on another set, in the same nerve, makes it breathe fast and shallow.

scenes.tts: Opposite outputs, from two subsets of one nerve. That is a reason to look for separate lines.
scenes.visual: The two traces side by side. Above them the shared grey cable stays whole and resolves into two coloured subsets.
scenes.narration: Opposite outputs, from two subsets of one nerve. That is a reason to look for separate lines.

scenes.tts: Here are three questions to ask of any population. First, what stimulus do the cells answer?
scenes.visual: Three empty columns build on screen, each headed by a question mark. The first fills with a heading: stimulus?
scenes.narration: Here are three questions to ask of any population. First, what stimulus do the cells answer?

scenes.tts: Second, what turns that stimulus into electrical current?
scenes.visual: Second column heading appears: channel? A small membrane channel icon sits under it.
scenes.narration: Second, what turns that stimulus into electrical current?

scenes.tts: Third, what changes when you drive or remove the cells?
scenes.visual: Third column heading appears: output? A breathing trace and a food hopper sit under it.
scenes.narration: Third, what changes when you drive or remove the cells?

scenes.tts: Driving a population tests sufficiency. Removing it and seeing the output fail tests necessity.
scenes.visual: Two small arrows into the output column, labelled sufficiency (drive it) and necessity (remove it).
scenes.narration: Driving a population tests sufficiency. Removing it and seeing the output fail tests necessity.

scenes.tts: Each question needs its own evidence. Some stay open for years. An answer to one does not by itself answer another.
scenes.visual: The three open questions held together, with a bar between them labelled: separate evidence. Caption: an answer to one does not answer another. One column is left visibly blank to show that a population can be studied with a question still open.
scenes.narration: Each question needs its own evidence. Some stay open for years. An answer to one does not by itself answer another.

scenes.tts: How do researchers get hold of these cells? With a genetic label, usually a Cree line.
scenes.caption: How do researchers get hold of these cells? With a genetic label, usually a Cre line.
scenes.visual: A handle icon appears beside the columns, attached to a cloud of labelled neurons. Label: Cre line, genetic label.
scenes.narration: How do researchers get hold of these cells? With a genetic label, usually a Cre line.

scenes.tts: A label is a handle on a population. On its own it answers none of the three questions.
scenes.visual: The handle icon appears beside the three questions, holding a cloud of labelled neurons.
scenes.narration: A label is a handle on a population. On its own it answers none of the three questions.

scenes.tts: Its name may identify a receptor or channel those cells express. Labelling alone does not establish the natural stimulus, the protein's causal role in transduction, or the output.
scenes.visual: An arrow from the handle reaches the channel column and stops short of filling it. Caption: labelling alone does not establish a causal role.
scenes.narration: Its name may identify a receptor or channel those cells express. Labelling alone does not establish the natural stimulus, the protein's causal role in transduction, or the output.

scenes.tts: One worked case. Afferents labelled by G P R sixty five answer food arriving in the intestine.
scenes.caption: One worked case. Afferents labelled by GPR65 answer food arriving in the intestine.
scenes.visual: A gut segment with villi; a labelled terminal inside one villus lights up as food enters the lumen. The stimulus column fills in: food in the intestine.
scenes.narration: One worked case. Afferents labelled by GPR65 answer food arriving in the intestine.

scenes.tts: Driving the same cells with light suppressed stomach contractions in an anaesthetized mouse.
scenes.visual: The output column gains a first row: gastric contractions suppressed, anaesthetized mouse. A stomach trace flattens.
scenes.narration: Driving the same cells with light suppressed stomach contractions in an anaesthetized mouse.

scenes.tts: This looks like a satiety line. Predict. In an awake mouse, what should driving them do to how much it eats?
scenes.visual: An awake mouse at a food hopper, with a question mark over the hopper. Output column, second row, left blank.
scenes.narration: This looks like a satiety line. Predict. In an awake mouse, what should driving them do to how much it eats?

scenes.tts: In the assays tested, driving them did not measurably change feeding.
scenes.visual: Stimulated and control mice eat at similar rates, with matched cumulative-intake traces running together. Caption: no measurable stimulation-related change in intake in these assays.
scenes.narration: In the assays tested, driving them did not measurably change feeding.

scenes.tts: One population, three answers. Yes to the stimulus, yes to one output, no to another.
scenes.visual: The three filled cells shown together: yes, yes, no. Label: one population, three measurements.
scenes.narration: One population, three answers. Yes to the stimulus, yes to one output, no to another.

scenes.tts: Every answer holds only for the organ, age, assay and anaesthetic state measured.
scenes.visual: A footer band under the columns: organ, age, assay, anaesthetic state.
scenes.narration: Every answer holds only for the organ, age, assay and anaesthetic state measured.

scenes.tts: Hold three questions in mind. Stimulus, channel, output. A handle alone answers none of them.
scenes.visual: Takeaway card: the three questions, with the handle icon beside them, touching but never completing any one of them.
scenes.narration: Hold three questions in mind. Stimulus, channel, output. A handle alone answers none of them.
